item.title: Introduction
item.description: This page describes the detailed IOC startup structure and the main classic entry points. If you want the shortest current path for a new configuration, start with Quickstart and Examples first. If any naming is unclear, see Terminology. Principle For a schematic of the EPICS, realtime-engine and EtherCAT layers, see How the layers fit together. EtherCAT requires the field bus components (slaves) to be configured on the master. The master must know about the data exchanges with the slaves, this is referred to as process image.

item.title: Terminology
item.description: This page defines the main terms used across the manual. Preferred terms axis PLC An axis PLC is PLC logic attached directly to one axis as part of the motion configuration. Use it for axis-local logic such as local interlocks, setpoint conditioning, or small axis-specific sequences. best-practice example A best-practice example is a public, reusable example under examples/PSI/best_practice/. item.title: syntax
item.description: In ecmc, PLCs are based on the exprtk expression evaluation library. For detailed syntax help, see the exprtk website. Companion pages: variables patterns functions best practice function libs As a general rule, prefer PLC helper functions over direct raw variable access when both are available. The function calls are usually clearer, more stable as an interface, and easier to search for in examples and documentation. This is also the better runtime choice: PLC variables are refreshed around each PLC scan, while function calls read the current value directly.

item.title: iocsh utilities
item.description: Scope This page documents the ecmc-specific iocsh helper commands that are useful in startup files and low-level commissioning. Most users primarily need: expression helpers such as ecmcEpicsEnvSetCalc conditional/script helpers such as ecmcIf and ecmcForLoop direct parser access through ecmcConfig / ecmcConfigOrDie ecmcEpicsEnvSetCalc ecmcEpicsEnvSetCalc() evaluates an expression and writes the result to an EPICS environment variable. item.title: general best practice
item.description: Scope Use this page for host-level and startup-level recommendations that apply across many ecmc systems. EtherCAT rate (EC_RATE) The default EtherCAT frame rate in ecmc is 1 kHz. item.title: EL1xxx
item.description: Scope Use this page for EL1xxx digital-input terminals with special timing or signal level behavior. EL1262 oversampling and NELM The EL1262 transfers its oversampled digital inputs as packed bytes. Therefore, for this terminal, NELM specifies the number of bytes per channel and per EtherCAT cycle, not the number of individual digital samples. The actual oversampling factor is: oversampling factor = NELM * 8 For example, NELM=1 transfers one byte containing eight time-ordered input bits, so it configures 8-times oversampling.

item.title: EtherCAT Endpoint Timing
item.description: Purpose ecmc describes when an input value was acquired and when an output will be applied. The same model is used for encoders, digital inputs, drives and digital outputs, with or without Distributed Clocks (DC). It is the timing base for control-delay compensation, touch probes and position-triggered outputs. Generic timing model TIME ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────► input event application anchor A[k] output event E_in ●───────────────────────────────●────────────────────────────────● E_out │ │ │ └── input age Δin (< 0) ────────┘──── output lead Δout (> 0) ────┘ sample → copy → PDO → Rx control calculation → Tx → apply endpoint delay = E_out - E_in = Δout - Δin input terminal generation selection: sample ── calculation/copy time ── ready ─────────────────────────────► │ PDO frame after ready ──────────────┘ uses this sample PDO frame before ready ─────────────── uses the previous sample calculationCopyTimeNs determines which PDO generation is visible.

item.title: Verify DC Timing with Position Compare
item.description: Purpose This example verifies a timestamp-scheduled output against a hardware touch-probe latch. It is useful when checking whether Distributed Clock (DC) timing, terminal phase, wiring and ecmc position-compare prediction are good enough for position-triggered outputs. The tested setup is: ecmc axis position compare -> EL2252 timestamp-scheduled output pulse -> EL7062/ED7062 touch-probe input -> encoder touch-probe latched position + timestamp -> optional PLC reconstruction check The EL2252 proves the output timing. The EL7062/ED7062 touch probe proves when the electrical edge arrived and what encoder position the terminal latched at that edge.

item.title: direction of motion
item.description: The direction of motion can be affected in several ways: on the slave level, in axis scaling, or in the EPICS motor record. The best option is to change direction at the slave level. The alternatives can lead to unintuitive scaling factors or mismatches between ECMC and EPICS. EtherCAT slave ecmccfg allows SDOs to be set in the IOC startup script or in dedicated slave configuration files. As most slaves have an SDO to invert the direction of motion or counting, it’s only natural to make use of this feature.

item.title: Native target-write motion
item.description: Native axes normally stage a target position and wait for an EXECUTE request. The optional target-write mode starts an ABS or REL move when the target is written. It is configured separately for each axis and is disabled by default. The axis can move without EXECUTE when this mode is enabled. Writing the native target-position PV starts motion, similar to writing .VAL on an EPICS motor record. Editing the target in a panel, writing it from a script, or restoring it from a saved value is therefore a motion request—not just preparation for a later execute command.

item.title: Drive output lookup-table compensation
item.description: Purpose A CSV axis can add a position-dependent feed-forward value to its drive output. This is useful for a voice coil working against a spring, gravity compensation, or another repeatable load that needs a non-zero command to remain stationary. The compensation is applied as: raw drive output = (controller output + scale * LUT(actual position)) / drive scale + raw drive offset Both LUT columns use engineering units: column 1: actual axis position, in the encoder/axis position unit column 2: CSV drive-command offset, in the controller-output unit The sum passes through the normal drive.

item.title: Encoder relay power control
item.description: Encoder relay power control reduces the time an absolute encoder, such as a BiSS encoder in vacuum, is powered. It is disabled by default and configured separately for each encoder. Existing axes keep their previous behavior. Power-off and wake-up After a move completes, the encoder stays powered until the axis has remained atTarget for the configured power-off delay. When a positive controller deadband is smaller than the atTarget tolerance, the axis must also be within that deadband.
